questions.question: Compare JPA/Hibernate vs JDBC vs MyBatis vs jOOQ for Java data access — when do you pick each?
questions.title: Data Access — JPA vs JDBC vs MyBatis vs jOOQ
questions.direct_answer: **JDBC (`JdbcTemplate`/`JdbcClient`)** is the raw-SQL layer — maximum control, zero ORM overhead, verbose for CRUD. **JPA/Hibernate (Spring Data JPA)** is the heavyweight ORM — productivity for CRUD and rich object graphs, but **N+1**, lazy-loading and dirty-checking pitfalls. **MyBatis** is **SQL-first** mapping — you own the SQL, MyBatis maps to objects; common in legacy DB integration. **jOOQ** is **typesafe SQL** via code-generated schema — compile-time validation, excellent for analytics and CTEs. Decision rule: **CRUD with relationships -> JPA; reporting/complex SQL -> jOOQ; legacy schema and stored procs -> MyBatis; hot path with custom SQL -> JdbcClient**. Real projects **blend** — JPA for 80% CRUD, jOOQ or JDBC for the awkward 20%.

interviewer_intent.testing: Breadth of data access options; honest trade-offs; when each tool earns its place; ability to blend tools intelligently
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: 'JPA everywhere' blindly; fighting JPA for complex analytics queries instead of reaching for jOOQ or JDBC
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss blending JPA with jOOQ/JDBC, N+1 pitfalls, Hibernate 6 improvements, Spring Data JDBC, and the 'wrong queries vs wrong tool' framing

sections.title: Four Dominant Styles, One Goal — Move Rows to Objects
sections.content:
Java has **four mainstream data access styles**, each sitting at a different point on the abstraction ladder.

**Raw JDBC** (modernized as `JdbcClient` in Spring 6.1) executes SQL strings against a `DataSource` and maps result sets manually or via `RowMapper`.
- **JPA/Hibernate** maps annotated entities to tables, manages a persistence context, and exposes JPQL, Criteria, and derived methods.
- **MyBatis** keeps SQL in XML or annotations and lets the developer own every statement.
- **jOOQ** generates Java classes from the database schema and exposes a typed SQL DSL.

Alongside these, **Spring Data JDBC** sits midway — aggregate-oriented, no lazy loading, no persistence context — and **R2DBC** brings reactive semantics. The interview question is rarely 'which is best' but **'which fits this workload'** — and increasingly, 'how do you blend them in one service'.

sections.title: Abstraction Ladder
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TB
    subgraph Raw["Closest to SQL, most control"]
        jdbc["JDBC / JdbcClient (raw SQL + RowMapper)"]
    end
    subgraph SqlFirst["SQL-first with mapping"]
        mb["MyBatis (SQL in XML or annotations)"]
        jq["jOOQ (typesafe Java DSL)"]
    end
    subgraph Orm["Object-relational mapping"]
        sdj["Spring Data JDBC (aggregate-oriented)"]
        jpa["JPA / Hibernate (full ORM, lazy, caches)"]
    end
    jdbc --> db[("Database")]
    mb --> db
    jq --> db
    sdj --> db
    jpa --> db
```

sections.title: Side-by-Side Across the Dimensions That Matter
sections.content:
Use this table to map a workload to a tool. The right answer is rarely a single column — it's usually JPA plus one of the others.

| Dimension | JDBC (`JdbcClient`) | JPA / Hibernate | MyBatis | jOOQ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Abstraction | Low (raw SQL) | High (entities) | Medium (SQL + mapping) | Medium (typed DSL) |
| Type safety | Strings | JPQL runtime | Strings | Compile-time |
| CRUD boilerplate | High | Very low | Medium | Medium |
| Complex SQL / window fn | Great | Awkward (native) | Great | Excellent |
| Lazy loading / N+1 risk | None | High | None | None |
| Caching | None | L1/L2 | Built-in | None |
| Performance | Best | Good with tuning | Near JDBC | Near JDBC |
| Best fit | Hot paths, procs | CRUD + relationships | Legacy, dynamic SQL | Analytics, BI |

sections.title: When Each Wins — Concrete Use Cases
sections.content:
**JPA / Hibernate (Spring Data JPA) wins when:**
- **CRUD-heavy domain** with clear entity relationships (orders, users, products).
- Team is comfortable with entities and `@Transactional` boundaries.
- Productivity matters more than fine-grained SQL control.
- You need `@OneToMany`, `@ManyToMany`, polymorphic queries out of the box.

```java
public interface OrderRepository extends JpaRepository<Order, Long> {
    List<Order> findByCustomerIdAndStatus(Long customerId, OrderStatus status);

    @Query("select o from Order o join fetch o.items where o.id = :id")
    Optional<Order> findByIdWithItems(Long id);
}
```

**JDBC (`JdbcClient`) wins when:**
- One critical endpoint needs **hand-tuned SQL**.
- You need stored procedure calls or DB-specific features.
- Batch operations where every millisecond matters.
- Migrating off legacy JDBC code without adopting an ORM.

```java
public List<OrderSummary> byCustomer(Long id) {
    return jdbc.sql("""
        select o.id, o.status, count(oi.id) item_count, sum(oi.price) total
        from orders o left join order_items oi on oi.order_id = o.id
        where o.customer_id = :cid group by o.id order by o.created_at desc
        """)
        .param("cid", id)
        .query((rs, i) -> new OrderSummary(rs.getLong("id"), rs.getString("status"),
                                            rs.getInt("item_count"), rs.getBigDecimal("total")))
        .list();
}
```

**MyBatis wins when:**
- Team **wants to own all SQL** explicitly.
- Legacy database with unusual schemas, stored procedures, or complex triggers.
- Heavy use of dynamic SQL based on input.
- Common in Korean/Japanese/Chinese teams (cultural prevalence).

```java
@Mapper
public interface OrderMapper {
    @Select("select * from orders where customer_id = #{customerId} "
          + "<if test='status != null'>and status = #{status}</if>")
    List<Order> findByCustomer(Long customerId, String status);
}
```

**jOOQ wins when:**
- Heavy reporting/analytics with **window functions, CTEs, complex joins**.
- You want **compile-time SQL validation**.
- Frequent schema changes — code-gen catches breakages.
- Building BI tools or query-heavy backends.

```java
Result<Record3<String, Integer, BigDecimal>> top = dsl
    .select(CUSTOMER.NAME, count(), sum(ORDER.AMOUNT))
    .from(CUSTOMER).join(ORDER).on(ORDER.CUSTOMER_ID.eq(CUSTOMER.ID))
    .where(ORDER.CREATED_AT.greaterThan(startOfMonth))
    .groupBy(CUSTOMER.NAME).orderBy(sum(ORDER.AMOUNT).desc())
    .limit(10).fetch();
```

**Spring Data JDBC wins when:**
- DDD-style aggregates with **no laziness**.
- You want repository convenience without Hibernate's footprint.
- You can model the world as load-modify-save aggregates and skip cache complexity.

sections.title: Blending Tools in One Service
Pros, Cons, and Hibernate 6 Notes
sections.content:
**When JPA helps:**
- **`save`, `findById`, `JpaRepository`** removes 80% of CRUD boilerplate.
- Mature ecosystem — Flyway, Bean Validation, Spring Data, auditing.
- Relationship navigation across object graphs feels natural.

**When JPA hurts:**
- **N+1 queries** when lazy collections are accessed in loops.
- **`LazyInitializationException`** when entities leave the transaction.
- **Dirty checking** triggers unexpected UPDATEs at flush time.
- **Native query mode** for complex SQL is awkward and untyped.

**When jOOQ helps:**
- **Compile-time safety** — rename a column and every query breaks at build.
- **CTEs, window functions, lateral joins** are first-class.
- Excellent for analytics and BI.

**When jOOQ hurts:**
- Code-gen step adds build complexity.
- **Commercial license** required for Oracle, SQL Server, DB2 (free for Postgres/MySQL).
- Verbose for simple CRUD.

**When MyBatis helps:**
- **Full SQL visibility** — no magic, no surprises.
- Dynamic SQL via `<foreach>`, `<if>`, `<choose>`.
- Friendly to stored procs and complex result maps.

**When MyBatis hurts:**
- XML drift — SQL diverges across mappers without strict review.
- No schema validation — column rename breaks silently.
- Smaller community in the West.

**Watch for (all tools):**
- **90% of performance problems are wrong queries, not wrong tool.**
- Hibernate 6 brings stricter JPQL, better streaming with `Stream<Entity>`, improved Criteria, native UUID.
- **Spring Data JDBC** is increasingly viable for DDD aggregates that don't need laziness.
- **R2DBC** is for reactive stacks; it does not replace JPA/jOOQ/JDBC for blocking apps.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **JDBC (`JdbcClient`)** — raw SQL, full control, no ORM; fastest, verbose for CRUD.
- **JPA/Hibernate (Spring Data JPA)** — high-productivity ORM; great for CRUD + relationships; N+1 and lazy-loading pitfalls.
- **MyBatis** — SQL-first mapping; team owns all SQL; common in Asia and legacy integration.
- **jOOQ** — typesafe Java DSL over generated schema; compile-time safety; excellent for analytics.
- **Spring Data JDBC** — middle ground; aggregate-oriented, no lazy loading, no persistence context.
- **Decision tree** — CRUD+relations -> JPA; analytics -> jOOQ; legacy+procs -> MyBatis; hot path -> JdbcClient.
- **Blending tools** is the production norm — JPA for 80%, jOOQ/JDBC for the awkward 20%.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Java has four dominant SQL data access styles, each at a different abstraction level.

**JDBC via `JdbcClient`:**
- Raw SQL with `RowMapper`
- Spring 6.1 fluent API; cleaner than old `JdbcTemplate`
- Maximum control, zero ORM overhead, verbose for CRUD

**JPA / Hibernate via Spring Data JPA:**
- Heavyweight ORM with entity annotations
- JPQL, Criteria, derived methods, native queries
- Productivity for CRUD and rich object graphs
- Risks — N+1, `LazyInitializationException`, dirty-check surprises

**MyBatis:**
- SQL-first; you own SQL in XML or annotations
- Popular in Asia and for legacy DB integration
- Friendly to stored procs and dynamic SQL

**jOOQ:**
- Typesafe SQL via code-generated schema
- Compile-time validation, autocomplete on every column
- Excellent for analytics, CTEs, window functions

**Decision rule:**
- CRUD with relationships -> Spring Data JPA
- Reporting and analytics -> jOOQ
- Legacy schema with stored procs -> MyBatis
- Hot path with hand-tuned SQL -> JdbcClient
- DDD aggregates without ORM complexity -> Spring Data JDBC

**Blending tools:**
- Real projects often use JPA for 80% CRUD plus jOOQ or JdbcClient for the analytical 20%
- Both share the same `DataSource` and participate in the same transaction
- Don't fight the tool — pick the one that matches the workload

**The honest framing:**
- 90% of performance problems are wrong queries, not wrong tool
- Hibernate 6 improves JPQL, streaming, and Criteria
- For new services in 2026, default to Spring Data JPA and add jOOQ or JdbcClient for the queries JPA makes awkward
